title: Best Free Open Source Browser Automation Tools in June 2026 (Updated)
summary: Compare 8 open-source browser automation tools for testing, AI agents, managed browsers, and web data, with practical guidance on choosing the right one.
body_markdown:
Playwright is our first choice for open-source browser automation when you need repeatable tests across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit. Selenium suits an existing WebDriver stack, while Puppeteer fits Node.js jobs such as screenshots and PDF generation. Choose Browser Use for custom Python agents or Skyvern for multi-step workflows that combine AI decisions with browser actions.


Updated September 24, 2026. These recommendations reflect each project's documented capabilities and current repository status. We publish Skyvern, one of the tools covered here. The sources below record what we checked.

Stars refer to the named repositories, not all projects owned by each vendor. They indicate interest, not task success. Language entries cover the main interfaces relevant to this comparison. A scripted library can also sit underneath an AI agent; the mode column describes its core role. Hosted products can add features and costs beyond the open-source project.


### The four approaches


Scripted frameworks execute browser steps and checks that you define. Playwright, Selenium, Puppeteer, and Cypress fit here. Start with this approach when you know the sequence and can check the result precisely.


AI browser agents interpret a goal and decide which actions to take. Skyvern and Browser Use fit tasks with conditional steps or changing forms. You still need a way to verify the output.


Browser infrastructure provides sessions that your code or agent controls. Steel belongs here: hosting a browser and deciding what it should do are separate responsibilities.


Web data APIs return content or structured records. Firecrawl belongs here, with additional browser interaction in its hosted product. Check the self-hosted feature list before assuming the same endpoints are available locally.


## 1. Skyvern: AI workflows across portals


Skyvern suits forms, downloads, and multi-step portal workflows. Its[AI browser automation](https://www.skyvern.com/) combines Playwright commands with actions directed by language and vision models.


How it works: Python and TypeScript SDKs support browser control, AI tasks, extraction, and validation. Teams can use the hosted service or run the open-source core.


Skyvern's product demo shows a browser workflow filling a form while the run tracks each action.


Setup and tradeoff: Self-hosting requires browser and model configuration. Some managed anti-bot features sit outside the open-source repository. Define a verifiable completion condition for each workflow.

## 2. Playwright: cross-browser tests


Playwright is our default recommendation for a new browser test suite. It supports Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, so you can exercise the same application across three browser engines.


How it works: You write the interactions and expected results. Playwright Test bundles assertions, test isolation, parallel execution, and debugging tools. The Node.js version includes its own runner for JavaScript and TypeScript. Python, Java, and .NET use their respective testing integrations.


Playwright's Trace Viewer connects each recorded action to the page state and debugging data from that moment.


Setup and tradeoff: Start with the language your team maintains, then define fixtures and expected outcomes. Trace and report tooling helps investigate failures, but your team still owns test data and the assertions that distinguish a correct result from a completed click sequence. It is a good fit for regression tests and repeatable browser jobs with explicit steps.


Project status on September 24: latest release **v1.63.0** , published September 4, 2026; **Apache-2.0** ; **96,627 stars** . Maintenance signal: not archived, with a repository push on September 24, 2026.


## 3. Selenium: WebDriver and existing test suites


Selenium is a strong choice when your team already uses WebDriver or needs to preserve an established test stack. Its core bindings cover Java, Python, C#/.NET, JavaScript, and Ruby.


How it works: Your code sends commands through the browser's WebDriver interface. Runs can execute locally or on remote machines. Selenium Grid distributes sessions so a suite can cover combinations of browsers and operating systems.


Setup and tradeoff: Selenium gives you control over the surrounding test framework, assertions, and reporting. That flexibility also means more integration choices. Start locally before adding Grid, and evaluate a migration against the cost of maintaining your existing suite. A functioning WebDriver stack can be a better investment than a rewrite prompted by a tool's popularity.


Project status on September 24: latest release **4.49.0** , published September 9, 2026; **Apache-2.0** ; **34,515 stars** . Maintenance signal: not archived, with a repository push on September 24, 2026.


## 4. Puppeteer: browser control from Node.js


Puppeteer suits JavaScript and TypeScript teams that need browser control inside a Node.js service. Common uses include screenshots, Chrome PDF generation, page rendering, and scripted navigation. It supports Chrome and Firefox.


How it works: Your application launches a browser or connects to a running instance, then directs page actions through Puppeteer's API. Chrome uses the Chrome DevTools Protocol by default; Firefox uses WebDriver BiDi. Some features differ between protocols, so check the documented support before choosing a browser.


Setup and tradeoff: Puppeteer fits a service that already has job scheduling, logging, and error handling. For a full test suite, evaluate how you will supply assertions, fixtures, and reports. Choose it when direct browser control is the main requirement and those surrounding pieces already have an owner.


Project status on September 24: latest **Puppeteer package release v25.12.0** , published September 23, 2026; **Apache-2.0** ; **95,620 stars** . Maintenance signal: not archived, with a repository push on September 24, 2026.


## 5. Cypress: testing your web application


Cypress fits teams testing their own front end. It supports end-to-end and component tests, with a command log and snapshots that help you inspect what happened during a run. Tests use JavaScript or TypeScript.


How it works: Cypress executes test commands in the browser alongside the application, with a supporting Node.js process. Its waiting behavior and visual debugging tools help developers investigate failures. Cypress also offers AI assistance for test authoring; that does not make every hosted feature part of the open-source app.


Cypress keeps the command log and application preview together so developers can inspect what happened at each step.


Setup and tradeoff: Evaluate Cypress against your application's component framework and browser behavior. Its documentation describes it as a specialized testing tool and lists constraints around controlling multiple browsers. It is a better fit for an application your team owns than for a general service automating unrelated third-party portals.


Project status on September 24: latest release **v16.1.0** , published September 15, 2026; Cypress App is **MIT-licensed** ; **51,027 stars** . Maintenance signal: not archived, with a repository push on September 24, 2026.


## 6. Browser Use: custom Python browser agents


Browser Use suits developers who want an AI browser agent inside a Python application. The open-source library accepts a task and model configuration, and can connect to a local or cloud browser. Hosted browser and agent services are separate options.


How it works: The agent uses page information and browser tools to work toward the requested result. Developers can add custom tools and request structured output. That makes it useful when the browser task needs decisions during execution rather than a fixed list of clicks.


Setup and tradeoff: Choose a model, supply the browser environment, and define how to check the result. Local execution gives you control over that setup; hosted services move some of the operating work to a provider. Compare complete runs on your own tasks, including model usage, retries, and review time.


Project status on September 24: latest library release **0.13.10** , published September 4, 2026; **MIT** ; **116,168 stars** . Maintenance signal: not archived, with a repository push on September 24, 2026.


## 7. Steel: browser sessions for scripts and agents


Steel Browser supplies browser sessions that an existing framework or agent controls. It is useful when you already have automation logic and need a service to manage browser processes, cookies, and session state.


How it works: Create a session through the API, then connect your automation to it. The project documents Playwright, Puppeteer, and Selenium integrations. Steel's documentation lists Python, TypeScript, Go, and Rust SDKs.


Steel treats each remote browser as an isolated session that existing frameworks and agents can control.


Setup and tradeoff: Steel offers cloud hosting and a self-hosted browser service. With self-hosting, your team owns service operation and upgrades. With either option, you still need to define page actions and verify results. Check the specific deployment's support for persistence, recordings, and other managed features before planning around them.

## 8. Firecrawl: web data collection


Firecrawl suits applications that need web content or structured records. Its API supports search, scraping, and crawling, with Python and JavaScript/TypeScript SDKs. The hosted product also supports browser interaction through prompts or code.


How it works: You request pages or a crawl and choose the output you need. Interactive sessions can add steps before extraction. Start here for content ingestion and research; evaluate the interaction features separately if the job must complete a transaction.


Firecrawl exposes scraping and browser interaction as API operations that return structured web content.


Setup and tradeoff: Self-hosting does not reproduce every cloud capability. The current self-hosting guide says the default stack lacks screenshots and page actions; these require a separate service. It also directs users to cloud or capability-specific requirements for Agent, Browser, and Interact.

## Plan a small-team browser automation pilot


Pick one recurring task, such as retrieving an invoice for a specific account and billing period. Write down what a correct result contains before choosing a tool. A completed run is not enough if it returns the wrong document.


Run the task more than once, including a case with missing data or an expired login. Record successful outcomes, time to completion, operating cost, and manual interventions. Include engineering time and model or hosting charges where they apply. Use the pilot to decide who will investigate a failed run and how the workflow will resume.


## How to choose


- Start with the outcome: an application test, a completed portal task, or collected web data.
- Match the tool to your team's language and the browser behavior the task requires.
- Compare the open-source component with the hosted feature set, including authentication and session handling.
- Check the license and maintenance evidence for the component you will actually deploy.
- Choose using verified results from your pilot, then account for hosting, models, retries, and maintenance time.


## Frequently asked questions


### Which open-source browser automation tool is best for testing?


Start with Playwright for a new cross-browser suite. Keep Selenium on your shortlist if you already use WebDriver or need its language bindings and Grid. Cypress is a useful option for teams focused on component and end-to-end tests in their own web application.


### Which tool should I use for a portal with changing forms?


Evaluate Skyvern or Browser Use when the task needs decisions based on the current page. Start with a bounded workflow and check its output, such as a confirmation number or the contents of a downloaded file. Treat a successful agent response as something to verify before relying on it.


### Is web scraping the same as browser automation?


Scraping collects content or data. Browser automation also covers navigation, form entry, and other interactions. The categories overlap: Firecrawl offers both data retrieval and hosted interaction features. Choose based on whether your task ends with data or requires a completed action.


### Do I need managed browser infrastructure?


A small job can start with a local browser. Consider a service such as Steel when session management and browser operations become substantial work. Your script or agent still needs to supply the actions and verify their results.


### Are open-source browser automation tools free to run?


Open-source code does not include free infrastructure or model inference. You may pay for compute, storage, browser hosting, proxies, or model usage, depending on the setup. Browser Use explicitly separates its free Python library from usage-based services; Skyvern and Firecrawl also offer hosted features beyond their open-source cores.
